title: Your pricing sheet, your price list and your 90-day plan

say: Your pricing sheet, your price list, and your 90-day plan.
This is the video for Module 4 of Introduction to Pricing and Selling.
This module brings everything together. First, a one-page pricing sheet that shows exactly how your price was set and why.

say: Second, the market range from your survey: lowest, middle and highest price per unit.

items: Date made and next review date

say: Third, the two or three benefits customers told you they value most.

panel.heading: The six parts of a pricing sheet
items: Date made and next review date

panel.heading: The six parts of a pricing sheet
items: Date made and next review date

say: Sixth, the date you made the sheet and the date of your next review. If any part is missing, your price is partly a guess.

say: Here is Ngozi's sheet. Every number traces back to a receipt, a timed batch, a market survey or a customer's words.
Her true cost is 550 naira a pack. Her standard price is 800 naira, a profit of 250 naira and a margin of 31%.
Her bulk price is 750 naira, and her walk-away price is 650 naira, which still leaves 100 naira profit.
She explains her choice in one sentence: 800 naira gives a 31% margin after paying herself, and sits in the lower middle of the market.

Check your sheet. Did you divide by good items? Did you include labour and overhead? Did you use markup and margin correctly? Is your walk-away price above cost? Are your input prices from the last month, not last year?
Then ask a trusted person to check it too.

panel.heading: Before you trust your price
items: Divided by good items, not total items
Input prices from the last month

say: Customers judge your price partly by how you present it. Share one clear price list with everyone, with the size, price and one short benefit for each item.
Keep the same price on your stall and your WhatsApp catalogue.
Answering DM for price makes some buyers move on. Prices that change from person to person feel suspicious. And reducing the quantity quietly without telling customers damages trust.
Sometimes your price must go up. Handled well, most regular customers accept it.
Ngozi's true cost rises to 600 naira. For a 30% margin she divides 600 by 0.70, gets 857, and chooses 850 naira.
Two weeks ahead she sends her regulars a short, honest message, and she honours every order placed before the date at the old price.
Her new margin is 29%, and most regulars stay.
A price is not set once and forgotten. Review it at the end of every month, using your weekly summaries.

panel.heading: When to review your price
items: On a fixed schedule, every month
When a main input price moves
When your margin falls for weeks

say: Recalculate that week if a main ingredient, material or transport price changes noticeably.

panel.heading: When to review your price
items: On a fixed schedule, every month
When a main input price moves
When your margin falls for weeks

say: Review if your margin drops below your plan for two or three weeks.

panel.heading: When to review your price
items: On a fixed schedule, every month

say: And review if you always sell out, or if sales slow sharply.
But do not change your price every week. Keep a price for at least a month, then decide with your records.

say: To remember. Put cost, market, value, price, offers and dates on one page, and explain your price in one sentence. Share one clear price list. Give notice before a price rise. And review your price every month.

panel.heading: Remember
items: One page: cost, market, value, price, offers, dates
Write one sentence explaining your price
One price list, the same on every channel
Give notice of increases; honour existing orders
Review monthly and when key costs move

say: Now complete your pricing sheet, make your price list and a sample increase message, and write your 90-day plan with review dates in your phone calendar.
You started with a price that may have been a guess. Now it is a real business skill. Continue with the lessons below.
